A SaaS product website needs a small set of pages that each answer one buyer question: what does it do, who is it for, what does it cost, is it safe, and how do I start. If you are a Pune startup building software as a service, those pages (a clear home page, a pricing page, a sign-up or demo path, documentation, and trust pages) do more for early customers than any amount of feature copy. This guide sets out what to build, in what order, and what to leave out for now.

It is written for founders and product owners of early-stage SaaS companies, and for the developers and designers who build their marketing sites. It does not give accounting or tax advice; for registrations and invoicing rules, speak to a chartered accountant. It also does not invent benchmarks. Conversion rates and sign-up numbers vary enormously by product, price and audience, so we describe what to measure rather than quoting a target.

## The Job of a SaaS Website

A SaaS site has two audiences with different needs. Prospects want to understand the product quickly and decide whether to try it. Existing users want to log in, find help and read updates. Mixing them badly is a common early mistake: a home page that tries to be a dashboard, or a login-first page that gives a stranger no idea what the product does.

Separate the two clearly. The marketing site explains and persuades. The application, usually on a subdomain such as app.yourdomain.com, does the work. Keep them visually consistent but technically distinct, so that a deployment of the product does not take down your marketing pages and vice versa.

## The Pages You Need First

### Home page

The home page should say in the first screen what the product does, for whom, and what to do next. Avoid slogans that could describe any software. A good test: show it to someone for five seconds and ask what the product is. If they cannot say, rewrite it.

Include one primary call to action, usually "Start free trial" or "Book a demo", and repeat it, not a different one each time. Show a real screenshot or short walkthrough of the product, not an abstract illustration. Add a short list of the main use cases and a link to pricing.

### Product or features pages

Organise by what the user wants to accomplish rather than by internal module names. "Send quotations in minutes" says more than "Quotation Engine". Each page should have a clear headline, a screenshot, a short explanation, and a link onward. Be honest about limits: listing what is not yet supported saves support time and builds credibility.

### Pricing page

Buyers look for pricing early, and hiding it entirely makes many assume the product is expensive. Even if you sell by quotation, show how pricing works: what drives the price, what a typical small customer pays as a range, and what is included. If you publish plans, make the differences between them obvious, state the billing period, and say whether prices include or exclude taxes. A short FAQ beneath the plans answers cancellations, upgrades and trial terms.

Do not invent discounts or fake scarcity. If you offer an annual discount, state the real figure.

### Sign-up or demo path

Keep the first step short. Ask for the minimum: work email, perhaps a name. Every additional field before the user has seen value costs you sign-ups. Our guide to [designing an enquiry form that gets completed](/blog/web-development-company-pune-enquiry-form-design-fewer-fields-mobile-validation-2026) applies directly. After sign-up, say clearly what happens next: check your inbox, here is your first task.

For a demo path, say how long the demo is, who will run it, and when you will reply. Confirm instantly on screen and by email.

### Documentation and help

Documentation is part of the sales process, because careful buyers read it before they commit. Start with a short getting-started guide, a list of common questions, and a contact route. You can grow it later. Make sure it is searchable by Google where appropriate, and keep a changelog so users can see the product is alive.

### Trust pages

Include an About page with real people, a contact page with a real address and phone number, privacy and terms pages written for your actual product, and a security page that states plainly what you do. Do not claim certifications you do not hold. If you collect personal data from users in India, see our guide to [DPDP Act website compliance](/blog/dpdp-act-website-compliance-pune-2026) for the website side of that, and take legal advice on the rest.

## Social Proof Without Invention

Early-stage startups often lack customer logos. Do not fabricate them. Alternatives that are honest:

- A short, real quote from a pilot user, with their permission and role.
- A brief case note describing a real pilot: what the problem was, what they did, what changed, with figures only if the customer agrees and you can show them.
- A line about the team's relevant experience.
- A "founding customers" programme, if it is real, with clear terms.

If you have nothing yet, say less and show the product. A convincing demo beats a thin testimonials strip.

## Technical Foundations for the Marketing Site

### Speed and mobile

Many first visits come from a phone. Keep the site light, serve compressed images, and avoid heavy animation libraries. Our guide to [Core Web Vitals and accessibility](/blog/website-accessibility-core-web-vitals-designer-pune-2026) describes the measurements to watch.

### Search basics

Give every page a unique title and meta description, a single H1 and a sensible heading structure. Our guide to [headings, alt text and semantic HTML](/blog/web-development-company-pune-image-alt-text-headings-semantic-html-seo-2026) covers the on-page fundamentals. Create a sitemap, and make sure staging copies are not indexed; the article on [robots.txt, noindex and staging sites](/blog/web-development-company-pune-robots-txt-noindex-staging-site-google-index-2026) explains how.

### Analytics you can trust

Decide your key events before launch: visited pricing, started sign-up, completed sign-up, requested demo. Track them in a way that does not inflate numbers; our article on [GA4 key events for lead-generation sites](/blog/web-development-company-pune-ga4-key-events-form-call-whatsapp-lead-tracking-2026) shows how. Respect consent requirements for tracking scripts.

### Security of the sign-up path

If the marketing site and the app share a domain, treat the sign-up form as a public entry point: validate input on the server, protect against bots, use HTTPS throughout and never put secrets in front-end code.

## Choosing How to Build It

There are three realistic routes.

- **A website builder or template.** Fast and cheap, and enough for a first version if your needs are simple. You may hit limits on performance, custom pricing logic and integrations.
- **WordPress or a similar CMS.** Flexible for content-heavy sites, with a large ecosystem. Needs care with plugins and updates.
- **A custom-built site.** More control over performance and integration with your product, at higher upfront cost.

A sensible approach for many early startups is to launch a simple marketing site quickly, learn what visitors do, and invest in a custom build once the messaging has settled. Rebuilding a site you do not yet understand is expensive.

We do not quote a single price here, because scope varies widely. Ask for a quotation that lists the pages, the number of design revisions, integrations such as a CRM or billing tool, analytics setup, and post-launch support. Our guide on [common mistakes when negotiating fixed-price contracts](/blog/common-mistakes-indian-smbs-make-negotiating-fixed-price-contracts-with-pune-dev-shops-202) covers how to keep scope clear.

## Connecting the Site to Your Sales Process

A sign-up or demo request is only useful if someone follows up. Decide where leads land, who contacts them, and how fast. Connect the forms to a CRM or at least a shared inbox with alerts, and keep a record of where each lead came from. If you plan to follow up on WhatsApp, collect consent clearly at the point of sign-up.

## A Launch Checklist

1. Home page states what the product does in the first screen.
2. One primary call to action, repeated consistently.
3. Pricing page with honest, current information.
4. Sign-up or demo path with minimal fields and a clear confirmation.
5. Getting-started documentation and a contact route.
6. About, contact, privacy, terms and security pages that match reality.
7. No invented logos, statistics or certifications.
8. Unique titles and descriptions, one H1 per page, a sitemap.
9. Key events tracked, with consent respected.
10. Tested on a real phone and a slow connection.
11. Staging site blocked from indexing.
12. Lead routing and follow-up owner agreed.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What pages does a SaaS startup website need?
At minimum a home page, product or features pages, pricing, a sign-up or demo path, getting-started documentation, and trust pages covering about, contact, privacy, terms and security.

### Should a SaaS website show pricing?
Usually yes, at least how pricing works and a realistic range or plan list. Hiding it entirely makes many buyers assume the product is expensive and leave.

### What can I show if I have no customers yet?
Show the product itself with real screenshots or a walkthrough, an honest quote from a pilot user if you have permission, and your team's relevant experience. Never invent logos or statistics.

### Should the marketing site and the app be on the same domain?
They can share a domain, commonly with the app on a subdomain, but keep them technically separate so that changes to one do not break the other.

### Do I need a custom-built site for a SaaS product?
Not at first. A builder or CMS can carry an early marketing site. Consider a custom build once your messaging and integrations are settled.
